description: Gallium is a chemical element with symbol Ga and atomic number 31, discovered by French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran in 1875. It is a soft, silvery metal at standard temperature and pressure with a complex orthorhombic crystal structure, and one of only four non-radioactive metals that is liquid at or near normal room temperature.
uses: Gallium is predominantly used in electronics, particularly in the form of gallium arsenide for microwave circuits, high-speed switching circuits, and infrared circuits. Semiconducting gallium nitride and indium gallium nitride produce blue and violet light-emitting diodes and diode lasers, and gallium is also used in the production of artificial gadolinium gallium garnet for jewelry. Additionally, gallium alloys with low melting points are used in thermometers as non-toxic alternatives to mercury, and gallium(III) compounds have been used in some medical applications including pharmaceuticals and radiopharmaceuticals.
characteristics: Gallium has a notably low melting point of 29.7646 °C (302.9146 K), just above room temperature, which is used as a temperature reference point on the International Temperature Scale. It exhibits a very large liquid range, with a boiling point of 2,676 K nearly nine times higher than its melting point, and has highly anisotropic physical properties that are strongly temperature-dependent. Unlike mercury, liquid gallium wets most materials and has a low vapor pressure at high temperatures, though its volume expands by 3.10% when changing from liquid to solid.
